newsitem.title: GUYANA: FEATURE-Guyana, an anomaly emerging from isolation.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Guyana, an anomaly emerging from isolation.

text.p: Guyana is an anomaly. Its African-sounding name, Anglo-Dutch colonial past, South American location, ethnic mix and colourful politics combine to create an odd cocktail.

"We're a small country but with big ambitions," President Cheddi Jagan told Reuters. A 78-year-old "Comeback Kid" as president, the former Marxist led his People's Progressive Party (PPP) to a striking victory at the polls in October 1992, the country's first democratic elections in 28 years.

Under his rule, Guyana -- wedged between Venezuela and Surinam on South America's northern coast -- emerged from two decades of self-inflicted isolationism. It is now back in the Caribbean mainstream with a fast-growing economy apparently firmly on the road to recovery.

The country's official name is still "The Co-operative Republic of Guyana" and the left-leaning PPP publishes an "organ" named "Thunder" but Jagan today embraces the free market system, admitting "there is no alternative."

That was not always the case. As premier of colonial British Guiana from 1961 to 1964, Jagan, a frequent visitor to communist Cuba, became a target of the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency. Race riots and U.S. opposition forced his ouster and meant his long-time rival, Forbes Burnham, would lead the country out of colonial rule in 1966.
Burhnam's People's National Congress (PNC) ruled for the next 26 years with a mix of state control and socialist experiments that, diplomats say, sent the country on a steady downhill slide.
DECAY IS OBVIOUS

In the leafy capital, Georgetown, decay is obvious. Some potholed streets are impassable, sidewalks are non-existent, sewers are clogged and power cuts form part of daily life. Horse-drawn carts and whitewashed buildings supported on stilts, some 150 years old, contribute to a "time capsule" sensation in what is the only English-speaking country on a continent dominated by Spanish- and Portuguese-speakers.

Guyana, for many outside the country, remains associated with the bizarre mass murder and suicide in 1978 of 914 cult members at a jungle enclave called Jonestown after their American leader, the Rev. Jim Jones.

Today, the tropical jungle has all but reposessed the sprawling Jones commune and nobody in Guyana likes to talk about the tragedy. "It left a bad taste in the mouths of all Guyanese," a leading journalist said.
Aware of Guyana's continuing problems, Jagan calls it "a shining example of a country on the way out of the abyss."
Most foreign observers and diplomats tend to agree.
"Guyana has had one of the most successful adjustment programmes anywhere," Charles Greenwood, the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) representative, said.

The economy grew by 7.9 percent in 1996 as the country -- at 83,000 square miles (215,000 sq km) nearly the size of Britain -- taps vast resources in agriculture, forestry and mining. Inflation, from a high 105 percent in 1989, fell to 4.5 percent last year, its lowest level since 1972.

With debts of $2.1 billion, the heaviest debt burden per capita in the world, Guyana in May won a major agreement from the Paris Club of creditor nations to reduce by 67 percent its debt with the Paris Club and the neighbouring island state of Trinidad and Tobago.
The deal "helped to re-establish Guyana's credit in the international financial community," an IDB report said. "By reducing country risk, Guyana is more attractive for foreign investment."
According to Finance Minister Bharrat Jagdeo, Guyana's economy today is "the freest in the Caribeean ... with no sector barred from foreign capital."
Greenwood noted that Guyana had no other option than opening up to foreign capital "because traditional aid pots of money (from the IDB and World Bank) are declining worldwide."
MANAGEMENT NEEDED

With only 800,000 people -- and as many more living outside the country, mostly in the United States, Canada and Britain -- Guyana probably needs all the help it can get. Years of emigration prompted by a grim economy and political repression have meant a shortage of managerial skills.

"There is administrative incapacity," Jagan admitted, saying it would probably take years to offset consequences of the brain drain of the 1980s. A foreign businessman summed it up harshly: "If you find a competent minister, you're lucky."
Guyana's problems, diplomats said, were compounded by deeply rooted racial antagonisms. "Party politics are played along racial lines," a European diplomat said.

The population is made up of descendants of indentured labourers brought from India in the late 19th century and descendants of African slaves. Indo-Guyanese slightly outnumber Afro-Guyanese and traditionally back Jagan's PPP.
The energetic Jagan, who confessed he would "most likely" seek re-election this year, said the opposition was playing the racial card "because they have nothing else to play."

"It's simplistic to say that everything is racial here," he said, insisting that race did not matter and, with the end of the Cold War, neither did ideology. But, reverting to the rhetoric he used when he headed an elected government in 1953, he said reforms must not endanger "social gains for the working people and the masses."

He seemed to acknowledge that his socialist dream would have to await another generation, "with the North-South dialogue being a dialogue of the deaf" right now, but he also spoke fervently of "a new global human order."

Broadly based on global debt relief and a regional fund to narrow the widening gap between the richest and poorest parts of the Americas, his plan calls for cuts in military spending and taxes on oil and stock and foreign exchange dealings.
"Jagan's dilemma is that he can't do what he wants, he can't state manage, because the country is bankrupt," a Western diplomat said.
